S1.title: Preparing for planned surgery
S1.text: You are scheduled for a planned operation. This video walks you through the preparation step by step: showering with antiseptic soap, medicines before surgery, fasting, which regular medicines are taken in the morning and which are stopped in advance, and what happens on the morning of surgery. We will explain why each step matters.

S2.title: Why clean skin matters so much
S2.text: Germs live on everyone's skin all the time. During surgery they can get into the wound. If an implant is placed in a bone or a joint, an infection around it is especially dangerous: sometimes another operation and a long course of antibiotics are needed. That is why the skin is prepared especially carefully before surgery.

S3.title: Showering with Septal Scrub
S3.text: Many hospitals in Israel provide Septal Scrub, a red antiseptic skin cleanser containing four percent chlorhexidine. If your ward provides it, wash with it twice: on the evening before surgery and on the morning of surgery, unless the staff instruct you otherwise. First, wash your hair with regular shampoo, and your face and outer genital area with regular soap. Rinse well. Wet your body with water. Apply about twenty-five milliliters of undiluted Septal Scrub to wet, intact skin using a sponge. Wash from your neck down to your feet, paying special attention to the surgical site, armpits, belly button, groin creases, buttocks and skin folds. Avoid the genital area, eyes, ears, mucous membranes, open wounds and irritated skin. Use separate sponges for different parts of the body. Follow your ward's instructions on how long to leave the lather on before rinsing. Rinse thoroughly under running water and dry yourself with a clean towel. Put on clean clothes and use clean bed linen. Do not apply creams, lotions or deodorant afterwards. If Septal Scrub gets into your eyes, rinse immediately and thoroughly with water. Seek urgent medical advice, especially if you develop eye pain, redness or changes in vision. If you have ever had an allergic reaction to chlorhexidine or another ingredient, do not use the product and tell the medical staff. If itching, a rash or redness develops during washing, stop using the product, rinse it off and contact the staff immediately. If your lips or throat swell, or you have difficulty breathing, call the staff immediately. At home, call an ambulance on one zero one. If your ward has not provided Septal Scrub, take a regular shower with soap. If you cannot wash yourself, ask the medical staff for help.

S4.title: Do not shave the surgery area
S4.text: Usually hair does not need to be removed before surgery. Do not shave the surgical area yourself: tiny cuts from shaving are an entry point for germs. If hair is in the way, it will be removed in the hospital with a special clipper.

S5.title: Premedication
S5.text: The evening before surgery or in the morning, you may be given medicines to prepare you — this is called premedication. For example, Vaben, a calming medicine that reduces anxiety and may make you sleepy. Omepradex lowers the acidity of the stomach contents. It is sometimes given when there is a higher risk of aspiration — stomach contents getting into the airways. It may reduce the acid effect, but it does not prevent aspiration itself, and not every patient needs it. All these medicines are prescribed by a doctor. After a calming medicine, do not get up on your own: call the nurse to avoid a fall.

S6.title: Fasting before surgery
S6.text: Before anesthesia it is important to reduce the amount of food and liquid in the stomach, to lower the risk of it getting into the airways. According to the Israeli Society of Anesthesiologists, you should wait at least six hours after a light meal, and at least eight hours after a heavy or fatty meal. Many wards ask you not to eat for at least eight hours before a planned operation. If surgery is planned for the morning or early in the day, you are usually asked not to eat after midnight. If surgery is later, the staff may move the start of fasting and sometimes allow a light early breakfast. Clear liquids — for example water, or tea or coffee without milk — are allowed by general recommendations up to two hours before anesthesia starts, and chewing gum up to two hours before surgery; it must not be swallowed. But the exact limits are set by your ward or your anesthesiologist: eat, drink and chew gum only as you have been told. If you ate, drank or chewed gum after the set time, be sure to tell the medical staff. If you have diabetes, slow stomach emptying, frequent nausea or vomiting, or you take injections for weight loss or diabetes, such as Ozempic, tell the anesthesiologist in advance — special rules may apply to you.

S7.title: Which medicines to take in the morning
S7.text: Fasting does not mean that all medicines are stopped. Some regular medicines should be taken in the morning with a small sip of water. These are usually heart medicines, for example beta blockers: if a dose is missed, the pulse may speed up and an arrhythmia may develop. Anti-seizure medicines: missing a dose can trigger a seizure. Medicines for Parkinson's disease: during a break, stiffness gets worse, and moving and swallowing become difficult. Eltroxin — a thyroid hormone. Asthma inhalers. Steroids, for example prednisone, if you take them regularly. Before surgery the doctor will check whether the dose needs to be changed or an extra dose given. Some medicines, on the other hand, are often skipped in the morning: for example water pills, some blood pressure medicines and diabetes tablets. Exactly which medicines to take in the morning is decided in advance by the doctor or the anesthesiologist. Bring an up-to-date list of all your medicines with their doses, and the packages themselves if you were asked to. While in hospital, do not take medicines on your own: agree on them with the medical staff.

S8.title: Blood thinners
S8.text: Eliquis, Xarelto, Pradaxa and Coumadin reduce blood clotting. Before some operations, they may need to be stopped temporarily. This is particularly important when spinal or epidural anesthesia is planned. Bleeding near the spinal nerves can cause serious damage. There is no single safe stopping interval for every patient. The plan depends on the medicine, its dose, kidney function, the type of surgery and the planned anesthetic procedure. The anesthesiologist and the prescribing doctor will decide when to stop and restart the medicine. In a few patients at particularly high risk of blood clots, the doctor may prescribe a temporary anticoagulant injection, such as enoxaparin, while Coumadin is withheld. This is called bridging and is not needed for most patients. It is not normally recommended when Eliquis, Xarelto or Pradaxa are interrupted. If you have a stent in a heart artery, tell your doctor. Medicines such as aspirin and clopidogrel help prevent blood clots, and stopping them can be dangerous. Do not stop these medicines without a plan agreed with your doctors, which may involve a cardiologist. Never change or stop your treatment on your own.

S9.title: Diabetes medicines
S9.text: Fasting and the stress of surgery can change blood sugar levels, so diabetes medicines need to be planned before surgery. Metformin is often not taken on the day of surgery. Your doctor will decide this. Jardiance and Forxiga are usually stopped at least three days before a planned operation. During fasting, these medicines can increase the risk of dangerous ketoacidosis, even when blood sugar is normal or only slightly elevated. Some tablets, such as gliclazide, are usually not taken on the morning of surgery because they can cause low blood sugar when you are not eating. If you take Ozempic or Mounjaro injections, tell the anesthesiologist well in advance. These medicines can slow stomach emptying. It is especially important to report nausea, vomiting or a persistent feeling of fullness. These injections do not need to be stopped for every patient. The medical team will decide whether any changes are necessary. During your hospital stay, insulin may be used to control blood sugar while you are fasting, having surgery and recovering. Your blood sugar will be checked regularly, and the treatment will be adjusted according to the results. If you have type one diabetes, you must continue to receive insulin even while fasting. This may involve an adjusted dose of basal insulin or a planned intravenous insulin infusion. Never stop insulin or change the dose on your own.

S10.title: Smoking
S10.text: Smoking reduces blood supply to the tissues, slows healing and increases the risk of infection. It is best to stop smoking at least four weeks before surgery. But quitting helps at any time.

S11.title: The morning of surgery
S11.text: On the morning of surgery, shower with Septal Scrub if your ward has provided it and instructed you to use it. Take only the medicines you were told to take, with a small sip of water. Take premedication only if it was prescribed. Remove jewelry and piercings, nail polish, artificial nails and makeup. Remove contact lenses and removable dentures, and your hearing aid if the staff ask you to. You will put on a hospital gown and wear an identification wristband. If any details are incorrect, tell the nurse. The surgeon may mark the surgical site with a marker. Do not wash this mark off. Before surgery, staff will repeatedly check at least two identifiers, such as your full name and date of birth. They will also confirm which operation is planned and on which side. Repeating these checks is an important safety step, not a mistake. The anesthesiologist will assess your condition, discuss the anesthetic plan and answer your questions. The surgeon will explain the operation, its main risks and possible alternatives. You will be asked to give informed consent before the operation, usually in writing. This may already have been completed at an earlier pre-operative appointment. Ask any questions before giving your consent.

S12.title: Key points
S12.text: The key points are simple. Shower with antiseptic soap if your ward provides it, or with regular soap otherwise. Follow the instructions you have been given, usually washing in the evening before surgery and again on the morning of surgery if possible. Do not shave the surgical area yourself. Take premedication only as prescribed. Follow your individual fasting instructions. On the morning of surgery, take only the medicines your doctor has allowed. Blood thinners and diabetes medicines may need to be adjusted or stopped in advance according to your doctor's plan. Before some operations, including spine surgery, staff may also use special antiseptic wipes. They will explain the procedure separately. Emergency surgery, for example after a hip fracture, may require different preparation. Always follow the instructions from your treating doctor, anesthesiologist and ward.
